status: Reviewed source-bound authoring portfolio: four fresh closures. Personal optional-use assessment and actual school-community advocacy remain distinct required conjuncts. No learner attainment or measured savings inferred.

eccc-generation.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada, dated2023-08-21
eccc-generation.readScope: Fresh complete actual main body read, including fossil combustion impacts and hydro/other renewable/nuclear discussion. Historical percentages, transition deadlines and absolute lifecycle-emission shortcuts are not adopted.
eccc-generation.role: Fossil-fuel combustion contributes air pollutants/greenhouse gases; infrastructure and community effects also matter for low-combustion generation.

york-factory.publisher: Keeyask Hydropower Limited Partnership, York Factory First Nation partner account
york-factory.readScope: Fresh complete actual partner biography and supplied historical statements read. No audio/video, linked community website or current office-holder verification. No quotations reproduced.
york-factory.role: Particular Cree First Nation: experienced earlier hydro developments, chose partnership after negotiations/referendum, and emphasises caution, water/land/wildlife and future generations. Its earlier relocation is described as following a trading-post closure, NOT falsely attributed to Keeyask.

keeyask-impoundment.readScope: Fresh complete actual impoundment/water-up explanatory body and dated2020 completion read. Linked info sheets/daily reports not inspected; no exact water levels or continuing local safety advice adopted.
keeyask-impoundment.role: Concrete construction-to-operation distinction: filling the reservoir changed upstream water levels. Do not claim all nearby lakes flooded; the source explicitly distinguishes locations.

keeyask-monitoring.readScope: Fresh actual introductory monitoring explanation and report-category list read. Hundreds of linked monitoring reports were NOT opened or claimed read.
keeyask-monitoring.role: Predicted/actual/unanticipated effects differ; Cree Nations and technical teams participate in monitoring. Presence of a report title is not proof of a harmful effect or proof mitigation succeeded.

metis-agreement.publisher: Manitoba Métis Federation and Manitoba Hydro, August3,2023
metis-agreement.readScope: Fresh complete actual English joint announcement read. French duplicate visible; underlying legal agreement not inspected.
metis-agreement.role: Acknowledged adverse legacy of hydro developments on Red River Métis rights and a long-term fund/dialogue/future-project process. Announcement is not proof all harm was repaired; no legal interpretation or claim of unanimity among all Métis.

innavik-main.publisher: Innavik Hydro / Pituvik Landholding Corporation project site
innavik-main.readScope: Fresh complete actual main explanation read: Inuit community leadership, October2023 delivery, diesel replacement and drinking-water monitoring. No images, linked water-monitoring campaign or underlying field dataset inspected.
innavik-main.role: Specific Inuit community Inukjuak: run-of-river generation replacing much diesel use, community leadership and expected benefits; water quality still requires monitoring.

innavik-benefits.publisher: Innavik Hydro / Pituvik Landholding Corporation project site
innavik-benefits.readScope: Fresh complete actual benefits body read. Source projections/aspirations distinguished from observed results. Exact emissions, worker counts, cost and future greenhouse outcomes not adopted as verified measured effects.
innavik-benefits.role: Construction versus operating work, reduced diesel dependence, social funds and possible diversification. Proponent account is a viewpoint, not independent proof that every benefit occurred or no environmental harm exists.

ieso-efficiency.publisher: Independent Electricity System Operator, Save on Energy
ieso-efficiency.readScope: Fresh entire one-page actual text read. No visual layout claim. Only unused lighting, natural/task light and possible electronic standby use adopted; heating, wiring, cooking and appliance-handling instructions not assigned to children.
ieso-efficiency.role: Even efficient lights use energy; some idle electronics draw standby power. Assess necessity and permissions rather than recommend switching off every device.

eia-carrier.readScope: Fresh complete actual explanatory main body read: secondary energy carrier and daily uses/history. No source imagery/video inspected; US percentages, invention priority and loose electricity-as-flow shorthand are not adopted.
eia-carrier.role: Generation transforms primary energy to electrical transfer, then receiving devices produce light/heat/motion; renewable/nonrenewable character belongs to source, not different kinds of charge.

eia-circuit.readScope: Fresh complete actual battery/circuit/transformer main body read. Only complete-path/load/open-switch account adopted; simplified battery chemistry/sign wording and transformer numerical theory are not used. No diagrams inspected.
eia-circuit.role: Closed low-voltage circuit supports current and energy transfer to a load; opening the path stops sustained current in the ideal simple circuit.

canada-generation-comparison.sourceSummary: Canadian combustion generation releases air pollutants and greenhouse gases. Hydroelectric infrastructure changes river conditions and needs environmental/community consideration; reservoir filling is a concrete change distinct from later operation.
canada-generation-comparison.attributionLimits: Original qualitative comparison based on source mechanisms, not a lifecycle dataset, current project recommendation or universal technology ranking. No child visits/handles generation infrastructure.
canada-generation-comparison.question: Original comparison cards: a Canadian diesel plant supplies reliable local electricity but burns fuel during operation; a hydro project requires construction and a changed river/reservoir while supplying electricity without ongoing diesel combustion. Assess immediate construction disturbance and continuing operation, and distinguish shorter-term local pollution from longer-term climate and habitat effects. Explain a benefit, a cost and evidence needed for each choice; use the named community cards below rather than treating communities as empty land.
canada-generation-comparison.expectedEvidence: Compare two generation technologies in Canada across society/environment, short/long timescales and climate. Explain mechanisms, distinguish direct combustion from total lifecycle effects and identify source uncertainty. Neither a renewable label nor electrical output alone establishes zero impact.
canada-generation-comparison.nearMiss: Labels hydro impact-free or treats carbon emissions, local pollution and river flooding as identical effects; discusses only one timescale.
canada-generation-comparison.changedCase: A hydro proposal reduces combustion but changes a river important to harvesting and cultural relationships. Revise the assessment without erasing those impacts or assuming a single emissions ranking settles all decisions.

first-nations-case.sourceSummary: York Factory First Nation’s partner account describes experience of earlier hydro developments and a later choice to partner in Keeyask after negotiation/member referendum, while emphasising responsible treatment of water, lands, wildlife and future generations. Reservoir filling and ongoing technical/Cree monitoring are separately documented.
first-nations-case.attributionLimits: Paraphrased institutional partner account, not invented community testimony or a legal consent ruling; no exact quote, current leadership claim or fish-consumption advice.
first-nations-case.question: Original source-analysis card names York Factory First Nation and Keeyask in Manitoba. Identify a construction/impoundment change, continuing questions for river/ecological/cultural relationships, and the community’s role in partnership and monitoring. Explain why choosing partnership can coexist with concern about effects and why a referendum by one community does not speak for every First Nation.
first-nations-case.expectedEvidence: Assess both participation/opportunity and responsibilities/risks over time with this particular First Nation’s attributed viewpoint. Distinguish documented changes, historical statements, monitoring questions and outcomes not yet established in the supplied material.
first-nations-case.nearMiss: Says all First Nations oppose/support hydro, that monitoring proves no harm, or that Keeyask caused the earlier relocation mentioned in a different historical context.
first-nations-case.changedCase: A report title mentions mercury monitoring but its results are not supplied. State what can and cannot be concluded; request actual findings rather than inventing fish contamination or complete safety.

metis-case.sourceSummary: The August2023 joint announcement acknowledges adverse effects from existing hydro developments on Red River Métis rights and describes a long-term fund, dialogue and processes for future developments.
metis-case.attributionLimits: Dated joint institutional announcement, not legal advice, the underlying agreement or a voice for every Métis individual/community. No unsupported specific environmental injury invented.
metis-case.question: Original card names the Manitoba Métis Federation’s Red River Métis account and the2023 agreement with Manitoba Hydro. Explain what acknowledgment of a continuing legacy and plans for a fund/dialogue show about long-term social impacts. Compare a new-project planning opportunity with a legacy from existing operation. Identify what the announcement does not establish about repaired outcomes or individual experiences.
metis-case.expectedEvidence: Treat Red River Métis as distinct from First Nations and Inuit, identify a source-supported long-term social impact and proposed response, and avoid claiming an agreement proves all effects were resolved.
metis-case.nearMiss: Substitutes an unrelated pipeline/transmission-only story for generation, groups Métis under First Nations, or calls an announced response proof of successful repair.
metis-case.changedCase: An original changed report says a dialogue process has started but provides no follow-up evidence. Explain why participation and an evaluated environmental/social outcome are different claims.

inuit-case.sourceSummary: Pituvik’s locally led Innavik facility in Inukjuak began delivery in October2023 and replaces much diesel use with run-of-river generation. The project describes construction/operating work, intended social opportunities and ongoing drinking-water monitoring.
inuit-case.attributionLimits: Project-proponent perspective, with source limitations explicit; no exact emissions savings, claim of unanimous support, practical drinking-water advice or invented community quotation.
inuit-case.question: Original card identifies Inuit residents of Inukjuak, the locally led project and diesel-to-hydro change. Compare construction-period jobs/disturbance with continuing diesel reduction, energy service, water monitoring and expected social funds. Distinguish reported operation from projected longer-term greenhouse/social/economic benefits; assess whose account is supplied.
inuit-case.expectedEvidence: Give an Inuit-specific account linking technology, community leadership and potential/observed effects across timescales, including climate rationale. Retain environmental obligations rather than interpreting clean electricity as no possible river impact.
inuit-case.nearMiss: Presents every projected fund/greenhouse benefit as already measured, assumes no monitoring is needed or substitutes Inuit for all Indigenous peoples.
inuit-case.changedCase: The proponent reports electricity delivery while a proposed greenhouse remains a possibility. Explain which outcome is established and what would be needed to evaluate the later claim.

responsible-use-school.sourceSummary: Unused lights and some electronic standby functions consume energy. Generation has resource/infrastructure effects even when its source is renewable. A safe choice depends on whether the service/device is necessary.
responsible-use-school.attributionLimits: The A/B/C rehearsal is hypothetical and supplies every needed condition. Delivery requires an actual teacher-approved recipient/channel; no learner work or school agreement is asserted beforehand. Children do not handle mains plugs/wiring or alter controls.
responsible-use-school.question: Original fully stipulated rehearsal: A is an empty classroom whose ordinary lights can be switched off by authorised staff; B is an idle display authorised for shutdown; C is a safety/accessibility device that must stay powered. Compare reducing A/B use with keeping necessary C, first when supply is modelled as fossil-based and then renewable-based. Explain why responsible use still matters. Prepare a real school-community advocacy message proposing an approved lighting/idle-device practice, with clear reasons, evidence, an acknowledged objection and a feasible request; actually share it through a teacher-approved school channel and retain that communication as evidence.
responsible-use-school.expectedEvidence: Assess school-use electricity choices from both renewable/nonrenewable sources using resource impacts and service needs, then advocate to the school community through an actually communicated proposal. Assess reasoning and communication separately; an unshared draft is not evidence of advocacy. No numerical savings or real school baseline is invented.
responsible-use-school.nearMiss: Says renewable electricity can be wasted without consequences, recommends shutting off safety/assistive equipment, or counts a private unshared draft as school advocacy.
responsible-use-school.changedCase: School staff explain that the proposed display supports a necessary service at certain times. Revise the request to avoid that use, and distinguish a communicated proposal from proof that a school policy changed or energy savings occurred.

integrated-electrical-principles.sourceSummary: Electricity can transfer energy from a source through a complete circuit to a load, where it is converted to other forms. It is distinct from creating energy from nothing or using up charge at a lamp.
integrated-electrical-principles.attributionLimits: Original qualitative reasoning models, not claims of an actual build, experiment or measured energy efficiency. Formal field/circuit equations and mains operation are outside scope.
integrated-electrical-principles.question: Original model cards: a correctly connected cell supplies a low-voltage lamp that emits light and warms; a switch opens that path; a hand-driven generator supplies a rated small motor; and a solar cell replaces the generator as input converter. Trace source energy, electrical transfer and output forms. Explain what the complete path/source/load do, contrast static stored charge with sustained circuit current using the existing electrostatics claim, and distinguish a conductor from insulating coating. Compare the closed and opened circuit without handling mains equipment.
integrated-electrical-principles.expectedEvidence: Give a connected account of electrical principles and transformation into/from other forms, with correct source/path/load roles and energy/charge distinction. An energy label alone is insufficient, and this reasoning task is not certification of actual building/testing, measuring meters, whole circuit vocabulary or every inherited child expectation.
integrated-electrical-principles.nearMiss: Says a lamp uses up electrons, electricity is created without energy input, an open simple circuit supports sustained current, or every device has only one output form.
integrated-electrical-principles.changedCase: The lamp stops when the source is disconnected even though all wires remain. Explain why a path alone is insufficient; contrast this with a hot lamp cooling after disconnection, where stored thermal energy can still transfer.

personal-optional-use.sourceSummary: Using an optional powered device for less time can reduce its energy requirement under the declared same-device/service and recharge conditions. Generation has resource/infrastructure effects under renewable as well as nonrenewable supply.
personal-optional-use.attributionLimits: Explicit original hypothetical learner-personal choice with stipulated energy/recharge conditions, not a measured saving, pupil habit or recommendation to remove necessary access. No child handles charging equipment, mains plugs or shared controls.
personal-optional-use.question: Original personal-choice card: during an optional leisure period, you may choose your usual permitted video session on a rechargeable tablet, a shorter session followed by a non-electric puzzle, or the puzzle for the entire period. In this model the same tablet otherwise switches off after your session, no one else needs it then, the puzzle uses the room lighting already needed in every option, and less tablet-on time requires less energy to restore the same battery charge later. An authorised adult handles any necessary controls/charging. Compare your own options, choose and justify one that reduces your optional electrical-energy use, and explain a possible tradeoff. Assess that choice first with the later charging electricity stipulated to come from fossil fuel and then from a renewable source. Explain why the energy/resource reasoning still matters under the second assumption.
personal-optional-use.expectedEvidence: Assess an explicitly learner-personal optional-use choice rather than only someone else’s classroom equipment. Link the shorter powered session/non-electric alternative to the stipulated lower subsequent charging requirement under both renewable and nonrenewable supply, with a reason and tradeoff. Protect necessary learning, communication, safety and accessibility use; this task assesses choices and does not require the child to control equipment or prove a measured saving.
personal-optional-use.nearMiss: Only proposes that staff switch off a shared display; supplies no personal-use option, says renewable energy makes any optional use impact-free, or sacrifices required communication/accessibility use.
personal-optional-use.changedCase: Now the tablet is required for an accessibility/communication service, or another learner needs it to stay on after your session. Explain why the original reduction cannot simply be assumed or imposed; protect that service and reconsider a different genuinely optional personal use. No savings or personal control of shared equipment is inferred.

actions: Supply all four named cases and distinguish facts, expectations and unknown outcomes.
Compare short- and long-term society/environment impacts of at least two Canadian generation technologies, including climate mechanisms.
Assess each distinct First Nations, Métis and Inuit case, with specific attributed community participation/perspectives and limits.
Use changed-case uncertainty probes; do not treat a renewable label, partner account or monitoring-report title as proof of no harm.
Supply the complete learner-personal optional-session case and require a justified choice under both renewable and nonrenewable charging assumptions.
Test the changed necessary-service/shared-use condition: protect access and revise the personal choice; do not require the child to control equipment.
Supply all three school use/need cards and assess responsible school-use proposals with resource consequences and necessary-service constraints.
Create a reasoned advocacy proposal addressed to the actual school community, using an authorised audience/channel and no invented savings.
Actually share the message, retain the communication evidence and revise a challenged choice; do not infer implementation or measured savings from advocacy.
Use the complete source-based generation and hypothetical use cases rather than child-code totals.
Evaluate generation and use across society/environment, benefits, harms, timescales and community viewpoints.
Justify responsible-use suggestions through mechanisms and service needs, including renewable-source resource effects.
Revise an integrated judgment after a changed condition; this overall authoring task does not by itself prove a learner performed school advocacy.
Supply all input/path/load/output cards and their explicit conditions.
Explain static-charge/sustained-current distinction and conductor/insulator roles through the existing component claims.
Trace transformation into electrical transfer and from it to light/thermal/mechanical outputs; distinguish charge flow from energy transformation.
Change source/path conditions and explain the resulting account; do not mechanically recertify every historical child claim or actual building procedure.

wholeCards.subject: English
wholeCards.name: Persuasive Writing
wholeCards.description: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence — including introducing claims, acknowledging counterclaims, organising reasons logically, maintaining a formal style, and providing a concluding statement
evidence: Write an argument essay with a clear claim supported by at least three pieces of evidence
Acknowledge and respond to a counterclaim rather than ignoring opposing views
Use linking words and phrases (however, furthermore, consequently) to connect claims, reasons, and evidence
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to convince you to let them stay up later, can they write down clear reasons and examples to support their case rather than just saying "because I want to"?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Communities Protecting Resources
wholeCards.description: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth's resources and environment
evidence: Describe at least three real-world examples of communities protecting resources or the environment
Explain the science ideas behind each example (e.g. solar panels convert sunlight to electricity, reducing fossil fuel use)
Discuss how individual actions and community efforts combine to make a difference
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe real examples of how communities protect the environment — like using solar panels, creating nature reserves, or cleaning up rivers?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Naming types of energy
wholeCards.description: Name and use vocabulary for types of energy and energy transfer — kinetic energy, potential energy, heat energy, light energy, sound energy, electrical energy, chemical energy, stored energy, energy transfer, energy transformation — and describe energy changes in familiar situations using these terms
evidence: Name the type of energy stored in a battery, a stretched spring, and a moving ball
Use 'energy transfer' or 'energy transformation' to describe what happens in a simple device such as a torch or a toaster
Distinguish between 'stored energy' and 'transferred energy' with a correct example of each
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stretches a rubber band and lets it go, can they name what type of energy it had when stretched — and what it changed into?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Conductors and insulators
wholeCards.description: Recognise some common conductors and insulators, and associate metals with being good conductors of electricity
evidence: Define conductors (allow electricity to flow through) and insulators (block electricity)
Test at least six materials and correctly classify them as conductors or insulators
State that metals are generally good conductors and explain why wires are made of metal with plastic coating
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} test objects in a circuit and explain why metal objects let electricity through but rubber and plastic don't?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: How energy travels around
wholeCards.description: Observe and provide evidence that energy can be transferred from place to place by sound, light, heat, and electric currents
evidence: Give at least one example of energy transfer by each: sound, light, heat, electric current
Explain that energy moves from a source to a destination through these means
Describe how electric currents transfer energy from a battery to a bulb through wires
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give examples of how energy moves around — like heat from a radiator warming a room, light from a lamp reaching your eyes, or electricity flowing through a wire?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Circuit vocabulary
wholeCards.description: Use technical vocabulary for electrical circuits — circuit, component, cell, battery, current, voltage, resistance, conductor, insulator, switch, series circuit, parallel circuit — and apply these when describing, drawing, and designing working circuits
evidence: Use 'series' and 'parallel' correctly to describe two different circuit configurations and explain the key difference
Apply 'current', 'voltage', and 'resistance' correctly in a written description of how a circuit works
Name at least six standard circuit components and describe what each one does
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know the difference between a series circuit and a parallel circuit — not just which one, but what actually makes them different electrically?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Static electricity and sparks
wholeCards.description: Explain static electricity as the build-up of electric charge through friction, describe how charged objects attract or repel each other, and relate static discharge to everyday phenomena such as lightning
evidence: Explains that rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another, creating opposite charges
States that like charges repel and unlike charges attract
Links the concept of static discharge to the formation of lightning as a large-scale electric spark
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a balloon rubbed on hair sticks to the wall, and connect this to the science of how lightning forms during a thunderstorm?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Climate Change Basics
wholeCards.description: Understand the basics of climate change: Earth’s atmosphere traps some of the Sun's heat (the greenhouse effect), burning fossil fuels adds extra greenhouse gases (especially CO₂), this is making Earth gradually warmer, and this warming changes weather patterns, melts ice, and raises sea levels
evidence: Describe the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere traps heat from the Sun
Explain that burning fossil fuels increases CO₂ in the atmosphere
Name at least two consequences of global warming: changing weather patterns, melting ice, rising seas
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the greenhouse effect in simple terms and describe how burning oil, gas, and coal adds extra CO₂ to the air, making Earth warmer and changing weather patterns?

wholeCards.subject: Science
wholeCards.name: Natural resources
wholeCards.description: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and that their uses affect the environment
evidence: Name natural resources used for energy and fuels (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water)
Describe how extracting and using these resources affects the environment (pollution, habitat loss, climate change)
Distinguish between renewable (wind, solar) and non-renewable (fossil fuels) energy sources
wholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain where petrol, electricity, and gas come from — that they come from natural resources like oil, coal, wind, or sunlight — and how using them affects the environment?

reviewLimits: All listed current whole cards freshly read; saved guide bodies have not all been freshly reviewed for this impact/principles portfolio. Existing rich research/provenance remains unchanged.

The old Computing digital-impact association remains preserved in the catalogue but is not counted as an independent general electricity/advocacy contributor. Persuasive Writing contributes the reasoned communication component without lowering its historical age ceiling or certifying the whole essay repertoire.

Actual school-community advocacy is a delivery assessment requirement. The source/task design supplies a complete rehearsal and real communication procedure; it does not invent completed learner work.
Technical and institutional source bodies support bounded factual contributions; original activity design does not establish empirical teaching efficacy.
